For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring the council replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.

The decision was the county's. A county rule now requires reflective letters on every road it maintains, and every road in Hollins Ford is one of them. Within a week the ambulance crews wrote to ask that the new signs keep Marrow's letter shapes. On forty years of night calls, they said, his boards were the first in the county they could read from a moving cab, and drivers who mistook turnings in other towns found Hollins Ford's streets on the first pass.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, found his patterns rolled in the old workshop: a full alphabet traced on brown paper. She asked the county to swap its standard letters for Marrow's, and the foundry cast every new sign from his tracings, enlarged by a fifth because the post office wanted larger letters. The care in those patterns shows best at the Gates, two of the first boards he painted. He gave the U of Upper Gate a long tail and the L of Lower Gate a heavy foot, and in four decades the crews never once mixed up the two Gates, even at night. When a delivery van struck the Upper Gate post in May, the post snapped where it had rotted, and the board came away whole, its edges as crisp as the day he cut them.

At a town meeting in June, residents voted to hang the old boards on the town hall stairs. They spent a fortnight in storage at the depot shed and then went up in street order, one landing at a time.

Marrow's boards earned their place on those stairs. Every driver who reaches Hollins Ford after dark still finds the way by letters he drew on Tanner Street, and the foundry did well to copy them line for line.

passage:
For forty-one years, every street sign in Hollins Ford came from one workshop. Elias Marrow painted them on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring the council at last replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.

What moved the council was a night last winter, when an ambulance crew was called to a house on Upper Gate. The driver mistook Lower Gate for it, as though the two boards had been swapped, and reached the house eleven minutes late. Marrow had given the U and the L the same looping stroke, and under headlights the two names blurred into one shape. The county had issued its rule on reflective letters nine years earlier, and the council filed it away and left every board where it hung.

It was a mix-up that anyone driving the town at night could have seen coming. Half the boards in town were rotting at the edges, and the Gates, among the first Marrow painted, had faded to grey on cream. Dora Pask, the town clerk, had put the county's rule before the council every spring. In the end the council struck a deal with the county for its standard plain letters, made a size larger because the post office asked for larger letters on the new signs. A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.

At a town meeting in June, residents voted to sell the old boards. The few who asked that Marrow's letters be kept on the new signs were outvoted, and after a month in storage at the depot shed the boards went to collectors.

The council should have taken them down the year the county's rule arrived and put up letters that a stranger can read at a glance, instead of waiting for an ambulance to prove the point.

For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal took their place.

The old boards came down because they were rotting at the edges. A county inspector found the soft wood in January, and the council had every board taken down that month, although the county's rule on reflective letters would have let them stand until they wore out. For six weeks the posts stood bare, and drivers mistook one corner for another at night, a mix-up that lasted until the new signs arrived. The boards went into storage in the depot shed, which the ambulance service takes over as its garage in November, and everything in it must be out by then.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, has asked to swap the stack into the dry corner of the shed, but the county's salt for the winter roads already fills it. The county crews struck in March over pay, so the boards were stacked in a hurry, and the two Gates, which hung nearest the river and came off softest of all, ended up at the bottom, where the roof drips. Marrow painted both of them the year he opened the workshop. Wood that soft can split under its own weight, and those two boards are carrying the whole stack.

The council will put the boards to a town meeting in October, where residents will vote on whether to hang them in the town hall or sell them for scrap. The new signs carry the county's plain letters, made larger at the post office's request.

If the vote goes against them, or simply comes too late, forty-one years of Marrow's lettering could leave the depot in a skip. Every week of rain through that roof works further into the bottom of the stack, and I doubt October will come soon enough for the two Gates.

For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal went up in their place.

For as long as anyone at the ambulance station can remember, each new driver spent a first night walking the town with an old hand, learning Marrow's boards corner by corner, and a driver who mistook a turning was walked round again until the mix-ups stopped. Residents knew the walkers by sight and would stop to point out the next corner. Those night walks ended in March, and the boards they were built around are gone.

The change began with the post office, which asked to swap the boards for signs with larger letters that its carriers could read from a van. The county's rule on reflective letters came into force a month after the order went in, and the new signs carry the county's standard letters. When the crews lifted the boards in March, most had rotted through at the edges and split as they came off. It struck me only later that the two Gates, which shared a post at the foot of the hill, carried the latest dates of all, pencilled the spring before he died and hidden on their backs for decades.

At a town meeting in April, residents voted to hang whatever could be saved in the town hall. The few boards that held together sat in storage in the depot shed through the summer, and in August they crumbled as the crew lifted them onto a truck.

I have walked the old route once since, from Tanner Street down to the Gates. On some evenings I still look up at a corner for the cream board and the black letters, the way you look for a face at the window of a house where someone used to live.

passage:
For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the street's name on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal replaced them.

The change began at a town meeting in January, where residents voted for new signs to match the ones on the county roads. When the two Gates came down in February, each had the other's name pencilled on its back. Arthur Venn, who drove the town's ambulance for thirty years, laughed when he heard and said he had known about the swap since his first night shift. Both lanes end in the same square, so he had always simply taken whichever one was nearer.

Dora Pask, the town clerk, turned the two boards over herself, struck the word Upper on her list, and wrote Lower above it. Marrow, it seems, had painted both Gates on the same afternoon in his first week and carried them out together. A visitor who mistook one Gate for the other arrived in the same square anyway. The county's rule on reflective letters covers only county roads, so the residents' vote was the whole of the reason for the change. It is hard to picture a happier mix-up than two boards hidden in plain sight on each other's lanes for four decades, with every driver arriving where they meant to go.

Only three boards in town showed any rot at their edges. After a week in storage at the depot shed, each old board went to the longest-serving resident of its street. The new signs carry the county's plain letters, made larger at the post office's request, and they went up on the right posts.

I laughed out loud when I read the council's notice, and again last week when Nora Hale of Lower Gate showed me her board hanging in her front hall, the word Upper facing the door.

The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun, and she had built both of them herself long ago. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way. Mrs. Pellow just handed me a veil and mentioned that she wintered at her daughter's in Lisle.

Soon I could lift a frame without flinching. One hot morning in July the sound of the nearer hive rose to a roar, and a swarm streamed out over the lilac by the back gate while my mother stared from the clothesline by our back steps. I found it settled high under the eaves of the shed. Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof herself and brushed the bees into a box, and we set it under the pear tree by her kitchen as a third, smaller colony.

What I thought about most, though, was the lane. Every evening the Corder brothers practised on Tamsin Lane, and every pitch that got past the catcher skipped under the fence and fetched up against the hives. Each time I heard the smack of a ball against the boards, I pictured the throw that would one day split a box wide open.

In August we took away the full frames. She sold the honey on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. Every evening she had me repeat what to watch for: the weight of a box, the colour of the brood, the bees at the entrance at dusk. On the first of September she put her hive tool in my hands and caught the train to Lisle.

Now the nights are turning cold, and until April the three hives are in my care. The smaller colony from the eaves still feels light when I tip its box, and on windy nights I lie awake wondering whether it has stored enough honey to last until spring. When the snow melts, the Corder brothers will be back on the lane.

The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun, and she had built both of them herself long ago. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way. Mrs. Pellow said that depended on how quickly I could count change on a Saturday morning.

Within a month I could lift a frame without flinching. One hot morning in July a swarm boiled out of the nearer hive, rose past the eaves of the shed, and settled in the lilac by the back gate, where I found it humming like a kettle. Mrs. Pellow carried a box out from under the pear tree by her kitchen, gave the branch one firm shake, and had every bee inside before my mother could cross from the clothesline by our back steps.

It was in her workshop that I learned what those hives were. She had cut every joint by hand from cedar, so closely that a knife blade would hardly slip between the pieces, and had sealed each roof seam with pitch she warmed on her stove until it ran like syrup. Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.

In August we took away the full frames, with the sound of the hives carrying in through her kitchen window. On Saturdays I stood at her table at the Brackwell market making change, while she told customers how the boxes were made. She still leaves the hives to look after themselves for a week each August while she visits her daughter in Lisle, and before the first frost she still climbs the ladder onto the shed roof to sweep off the leaves.

Those two hives stand against the fence to this day, and she keeps them still. I have built six hives of my own since, all to her pattern, and the best of them is a shade less square than either of hers.

The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees, and that summer her bees turned up in the oddest places. Her two hives, Agatha and Bertram, stood against the fence along Tamsin Lane, in a spot she had chosen for the morning sun. She had built both of them herself long ago and meant to have two more boxes ready by August. When my mother heard, she asked her whether I would be in the way, and Mrs. Pellow put a hammer in my hand.

In July a swarm left Bertram, sailed over the lilac by the back gate, and settled on the clothesline by our back steps, right among my mother's pillowcases. I found it hanging there like a brown woollen sock, and I laughed so hard that I had to sit down on the steps. Mrs. Pellow, laughing too, fetched one of our new boxes from under the eaves of the shed, shook the pillowcase over it, and set the swarm beside the pear tree by her kitchen.

On Saturdays she sold the honey at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. Her pitch to every customer went the same way: she held up a jar, named the hive it came from as though introducing a cousin, and winked at me over the buyer's shoulder. One morning a bee rode all the way to Brackwell in the jar crate and climbed out onto the table in time to be introduced.

In August we took away the full frames, with the sound of the hives drifting in through the screen door. When she visited her sister for a week, she left the hives in my mother's care, and every morning my mother found Agatha's bees drinking from the china duck in our birdbath. The day she came home, Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof and found two more asleep in the gutter.

She keeps them still, and they are still called Agatha and Bertram. Whenever a jar marked Bertram turns up on my mother's table, I grin all over again at that swarm hanging among the pillowcases.

The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives sat on the roof of her shed, a spot she had chosen years before to lift the bees above the fence along Tamsin Lane, and she had built both of them herself long ago. By that spring her knees stopped her at the third rung of the ladder. When my mother heard about the lessons, she asked her whether I would be in the way.

So it was I who climbed onto the shed roof each morning with the smoker, while she called instructions up from the yard. In July a swarm poured out of the far hive and settled in the pear tree by her kitchen, where I found it hanging from a low branch. We shook it into a box under the lilac by the back gate, with my mother watching from the clothesline by our back steps, while a few last bees circled under the eaves of the shed.

On still evenings the sound of those two hives carried down into the yard, and I used to lie in the grass beside the shed and listen until the light went. It was the first thing I listened for each morning and the last each night. I would give a great deal to hear the pitch of that hum again, low and steady, climbing a little on the hottest afternoons.

In August we took away the full frames and spun out the honey in her kitchen. She sold it on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. In September, with the ladder beyond her, she gave both hives into the care of a keeper in Dunmore, and his truck took them away one grey morning before school.

The roof of the shed has been bare ever since, and the box we hived the swarm in went with the others. When I walk down Tamsin Lane in summer, I still stop at her gate for a moment, listening for a sound that went away to Dunmore long ago.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. My mother had asked her in June to find me something to do besides lie on the porch, and the next morning a spare veil was waiting on our back steps. Mrs. Pellow's two hives sat on the roof of her shed, a spot she had chosen to keep the bees above the fence along Tamsin Lane, and she had built both of them herself long ago.

By July I could lift a frame without flinching, and every morning Mrs. Pellow climbed the ladder onto the shed roof beside me. Late that month a swarm poured off the roof, passed over the lilac by the back gate, and settled on the fence along Tamsin Lane, above the walk to the pool, where I found it at noon. My mother came from the clothesline by our back steps to turn people back, while Mrs. Pellow fetched a box from under the eaves of the shed and set the swarm beneath the pear tree by her kitchen.

The pitch of that roof was far too steep for hives, and on July afternoons the sun beat on the boxes until the wax went soft and the bees hung out of the entrances in sheets. Every inspection meant carrying frames down the ladder and back up again, which took twice as long as it should have and left the bees quick to sting.

In August we took away the full frames and spun out the honey. She sold it on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. From our porch I could hear the sound of the hives over the traffic on the lane, and in winter she left them up on the roof, where the wind off the hill struck them full on.

Hives belong on level ground in afternoon shade, and hers should have stood behind the shed, where the lilac would have kept the sun off them and nobody would have needed a ladder. She kept them on that roof every summer afterwards.

Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she asked Theo to get his teammates to shout less, then moved their work to the far corner of the park, right against the fairground fence. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, watched one recall and told Mara to keep her hands still at her sides. Just before calling, Mara's right hand had been lifting an inch.

That inch explained something the shelter staff had told her in April. Before Rook was surrendered, he had lived for two years with a man who called him all day in the same flat, bored pitch but waved an arm only when he truly wanted the dog to come. Rook had learned to tune out the voice and watch for the hand. All summer he had been reading Mara's.

On the morning of the trial, the loudspeaker crackled overhead just as Mara gave the stay command softly and walked away, but she kept her hands flat against her jeans, and Rook sat like a stone until she called. The judge awarded Rook a green ribbon. On the way to the car, Theo, still carrying the liver treats, asked what she planned to do with it. "I'm pinning it on Mrs. Ostrander's board at the shelter, because she saw the one thing I was doing wrong when I couldn't see it myself."

Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead. Then the streetlights on the hill come on, and the first swifts drop into the chimney, each with a sharp bank to the left, while the last bus passes the school gates.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. Those notebooks are the reason the chimney is still standing.

The storm two winters ago split the chimney with a crack from its top to the roofline. The council proposed having it pulled down, since a proper repair would cost more than demolition. Reyburn went to the March meeting, he told me, only to ask whether the work could wait until the swifts had left, and he set his notebooks on the table because he had carried them in. The councillors read them through and voted to keep the chimney standing for the swifts.

The masons who mended it chose lime mortar matched to the old, knowing that cheap cement would crack the soft brick and dry too smooth for a swift's claws. A century after it was built, the chimney stands as straight and sound as the day its last brick was laid, the best-made thing on the hill.

Whoever laid that brick built well enough for a furnace and, a hundred years on, well enough for six thousand swifts. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand over the empty schoolyard until they return in May, as solid as it has always been.

The council should have paid for lime mortar matched to the old brick, which stays rough enough for a swift to grip. In early October the birds will leave for the south, and before they return in May that stripe of cement should be cut out and redone.

Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School, after a day of feeding along the far bank of the River Wenn. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his totals fill four notebooks. This year's best, 6,140, is the largest roost he has ever recorded. The council has asked to see every page of the notebooks before it meets in January.

The storm two winters ago opened a crack from the chimney's top toward the roofline, and every month since, Reyburn has gone up the roof ladder to pencil a mark at its lower end. Each new mark sits a little below the last. In January the council will vote on whether to pay for a repair in lime mortar, which the masons say the old brick needs in place of cheap cement, or to have the chimney pulled down. Reyburn expects the vote to go the swifts' way.

I am less sure. If the vote goes the other way, or a winter gale finds the crack first, the swifts will come back in May to an empty patch of sky above a heap of brick.

In early October the birds will leave for the south. On every windy night since the storm I have lain awake listening for the sound of falling brick from the hill, and each morning I look out to see whether the chimney is still standing.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and in May they will return to the same stump. Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.

Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank on Mill Street pulls down its shutters, the church clock strikes seven and the last children leave the schoolyard, and still the birds wheel overhead in a dark, turning cloud. Then the last bus passes the school gates, and the whole cloud pours down into the chimney like smoke running backwards; by the time the streetlights on the hill come on, the sky is clear.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit the school's furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed, eleven years ago. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds. Of all his stories, the one he tells most often is about that furnace.

It was the first September after the school closed. Walking home past Linden Row at dusk, Reyburn saw a dark plume over the chimney, ran to the boiler room with a fire bucket, and flung open the furnace door to find the grate cold and swifts pattering down the flue. He tells it laughing, and he always slaps his knee at the part with the bucket. When the storm two winters ago put a crack near the chimney's top, the council voted to mend it, just as Reyburn had said it would, and the masons did the work in lime mortar rather than cheap cement, rough as the old brick.

I laughed out loud the first evening I saw it myself: a chimney that has burned nothing for eleven years, drawing a cloud of smoke down into itself.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and the chimney will stand cold until they return in May. Until they go, every clear evening the old chimney smokes in reverse over the schoolyard, and I stand at the gate grinning up at it.
